title: Real vs. personal property
body: Real property is the land, anything permanently attached to it, and the owner's bundle of rights. Personal property moves.
example: A Henderson seller's built-in pool goes with the house. The patio furniture beside it does not.
hook: If it moves, it's personal. If it's part of the place, it's real.

title: Is it a fixture?
body: When an item gets attached, courts ask: how it was attached, whether it was adapted to the property, the relationship of the parties, what the person intended, and whether there's a written agreement. Intent carries the most weight.
example: A Reno seller wants to keep a wall-mounted TV. Put the exclusion in writing.

title: Trade fixtures and emblements
body: A commercial tenant's business equipment stays the tenant's property. The tenant removes it before the lease ends and repairs the damage. Annual crops a tenant planted are emblements, and the tenant may harvest them.
example: A Las Vegas pizzeria bolts in its oven. At lease end, the oven leaves with the tenant.
hook: Trade fixtures travel with the trade.

title: What makes land different
body: Physically, land is immobile, indestructible, and unique. Economically, it is scarce, improvements change its value, investments in it are long-term, and location preference drives price.
example: Two identical floor plans in Summerlin can sell for different prices because one backs a golf course.
hook: Land is I-I-U: immobile, indestructible, unique.

title: Three ways to describe land
body: Metes and bounds walks the boundary from a point of beginning and back. Lot and block points to a recorded subdivision plat. The rectangular survey grids land into townships and sections. A street address is never a legal description.
example: Most Las Vegas tract homes are described by lot and block.
hook: Metes and bounds must come home.

title: Township and section math
body: A township is 6 miles square and holds 36 sections. A section is 1 square mile, or 640 acres. An acre is 43,560 square feet. To find acres in a description, start with 640 and multiply by each fraction.
example: The NE 1/4 of the SW 1/4 is 640 × 1/4 × 1/4 = 40 acres.

title: Liens
body: A lien secures a debt with property. Specific liens hit one property: mortgages, property taxes, mechanic's liens. General liens hit everything the debtor owns: judgments, IRS liens. Property taxes and special assessments get paid first. Most others rank by recording date.
example: An unpaid Reno contractor files a mechanic's lien on the house they remodeled.
hook: Taxes take the front seat. Everyone else lines up by recording date.

title: Easements
body: An easement is a right to use someone else's land. Appurtenant easements benefit a neighboring parcel (dominant) and burden another (servient), and they run with the land. Easements in gross benefit a person or company, like a utility.
example: A Lake Tahoe cabin's driveway crosses the neighbor's lot. Sell either lot and the easement stays.

title: Licenses and encroachments
body: A license is personal, revocable permission to use land. It's not an interest in the land. An encroachment is an improvement that crosses onto a neighbor's lot. A survey usually finds it.
example: A Henderson buyer's survey shows the neighbor's fence sits two feet onto the lot.
hook: A license is a permission slip. An encroachment is a trespass that stayed.

title: Fee simple estates
body: Fee simple absolute is the most complete ownership: unlimited, inheritable, no strings. A defeasible fee can be lost. "So long as" language ends ownership automatically when the condition breaks. "But if" language requires the grantor to act.
example: Land deeded to a Carson City church "so long as" it's used for worship reverts if it becomes a parking lot.
hook: "So long as" snaps back. "But if" needs a push.

title: Life estates
body: A life estate lasts for someone's lifetime. When it ends, the property goes to a named remainderman or reverts to the grantor. The life tenant may live there, rent it, or sell the life interest, but may not commit waste.
example: A mother deeds her Reno home to her son for life, then to her granddaughter. The granddaughter is the remainderman.
hook: Remainder goes forward. Reversion goes back.

title: Leasehold estates
body: Tenants hold leaseholds, not freeholds. An estate for years has a fixed end and needs no notice. A periodic tenancy renews until someone gives notice. A tenancy at will has no set term. A tenancy at sufferance is a holdover without consent.
example: A Las Vegas tenant stays past the lease end without permission: tenancy at sufferance.
hook: Years ends itself. Periodic repeats. Will is whenever. Sufferance is uninvited.

title: Severalty and tenancy in common
body: Severalty means one owner. Tenants in common own undivided shares that can be unequal, can sell without permission, and pass their share to heirs. There is no survivorship.
example: Two friends buy a Reno duplex 60/40 as tenants in common. If one dies, that share goes to their heirs.

title: Joint tenancy
body: Joint tenants own equal shares with right of survivorship. Creating one takes four unities: possession, interest, time, and title. If one joint tenant sells, the buyer becomes a tenant in common with the others.
example: Three siblings own a Henderson home as joint tenants. One dies, and the other two own it all.
hook: PITT: break a unity, break the survivorship.

title: Entities and trusts
body: A corporation owns property in severalty. LLC members get limited liability and flexible taxes. Limited partners risk only their investment. In a trust, the trustor creates it, the trustee holds legal title, and the beneficiary benefits.
example: A Las Vegas investor holds rentals in an LLC to separate them from personal assets.
hook: Trustor sets it up. Trustee holds it. Beneficiary enjoys it.

title: Condominiums
body: A condo owner holds fee title to the unit plus an undivided share of the common elements. Each unit has its own deed, mortgage, and tax bill. A recorded declaration creates the condo, and the association collects assessments.
example: A high-rise owner near the Strip owns unit 2104 and shares the pool and lobby.
hook: Condo: own the box, share the rest.

title: Cooperatives
body: In a co-op, a corporation owns the building. Residents buy shares and get a proprietary lease to a unit. There's usually one blanket mortgage, so if neighbors stop paying, everyone else may have to cover.
example: A buyer comparing a co-op and a condo learns the co-op board must approve them first.
hook: Co-op: you own stock, not a unit.

title: PUDs and timeshares
body: In a PUD, you own your lot and home, and the association owns the common areas. A timeshare estate is real property ownership of a recurring time slot. A timeshare use is only the right to use it.
example: A Henderson PUD owner owns the house and yard. The association owns the park and the gate.
hook: A timeshare estate owns a slice of time. A timeshare use rents it.
